0.title: Jesus and the Apostles: One Gospel, Two Moments
0.essay:
Read the four Gospels and then turn to Paul’s letters, and an honest reader may quietly wonder: is this the same message? Jesus walks the roads of Galilee announcing, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand” (Mark 1:15). Paul preaches “that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3), and unfolds justification by faith. Jesus preaches the kingdom; the apostles preach him.

The wedge

For more than a century, sceptical scholars have driven a wedge into that gap. Adolf von Harnack argued that Jesus taught a simple religion of the fatherhood of God and the value of the soul, which the church later buried under doctrine. William Wrede went further and called Paul “the second founder of Christianity”, as if the gospel of grace and the cross were Paul’s invention laid over a simpler Jesus. Today the same instinct survives in a softer form: the “red-letter” habit that prizes the words of Jesus and treats the apostles’ letters as a lesser, more complicated appendix.

One gospel, two moments

This study answers the wedge — not by flattening the real differences, but by putting them where they belong. There are not two gospels. There is one gospel, proclaimed at two moments in the drama of redemption. Before the cross, Jesus announces the kingdom that is arriving; he is the King, and he speaks of his death in shadow and promise. After the cross and the empty tomb, the apostles announce the kingdom that has arrived: the King has been enthroned through his death and resurrection, and they proclaim what he accomplished. The difference is the difference between “at hand” and “It is finished”.

And the deepest truth is more thrilling than the sceptics guessed. Jesus is not merely the first preacher of the gospel; he is its content. He came proclaiming the good news, and he came to be the good news. When we learn to hear the Gospels and the Epistles as one voice, the Bible opens like a single unbroken song: the King who announced his reign, reigning now from a throne that was once a cross.

The chapters

Two Gospels? — the wedge between Jesus and the apostles; “The Kingdom Is at Hand” — Jesus’ own proclamation; The Hinge — cross, resurrection and Pentecost; The Apostolic Kerygma — “Christ died for our sins”; One Gospel, Two Moments — the deep unity; and Guarding the One Gospel Today.

1.title: Two Gospels? — The Wedge Between Jesus and the Apostles
1.essay:
The suspicion is old and stubborn: the simple prophet of Nazareth was one thing, and the church that grew up around him another. Jesus preached a kingdom of love and mercy, it is said; his followers turned him into a sacrifice and built a theology he never taught.

Why the wedge feels plausible

Harnack put it memorably: “the Gospel, as Jesus proclaimed it, has to do with the Father only and not with the Son.” Strip away the later doctrine, he urged, and you find a religion of the heart. Wrede’s verdict on Paul was blunter: he was a “second founder”, and the stronger of the two.

The wedge feels plausible because the surface really does differ. Jesus rarely says in so many words, “Believe in me and your sins will be forgiven, for I will die in your place.” Paul rarely quotes the parables. The Gospels are full of Galilee, crowds, healings and the kingdom; the Epistles are full of the cross, justification, the church and the risen Lord. A reader who has never been shown how they fit can be forgiven for feeling the seam.

Paul’s own answer

But the wedge cannot survive contact with the texts. Paul insists that his gospel is not his own construction: “For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:12). He does not claim to have improved on Jesus, or to have embellished something the earlier apostles told him. He claims the gospel came from Christ himself — the same Christ who taught in Galilee, now teaching Paul from glory.

That is why he can say, “But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8). A gospel that was merely human could be revised and softened to taste. A gospel received from the Lord is fixed; it can only be guarded or betrayed. The man accused of inventing a second gospel is the very man who says there is only one, and that it came from Christ.

A truer sight of the same Jesus

One verse is sometimes misread as if Paul dismissed the earthly Jesus in favour of a heavenly idea: “Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer” (2 Corinthians 5:16). He means the opposite. Paul once sized Jesus up by worldly standards and judged him a failed, cursed pretender, and so persecuted his church. The cross and resurrection shattered that estimate. Now he knows the same Jesus rightly, as the crucified and risen Lord. The change is in the eyes that see, not in the Saviour who is seen.

Jesus’ own commission

More decisive still, it was Jesus who commissioned the apostolic message. On the evening of the resurrection he opened the Scriptures and said, “Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations” (Luke 24:46–47). Every element of the later apostolic sermons is already here: the Christ must suffer; he rises on the third day; and in his name repentance and forgiveness are to be preached to the nations. Read the sermons in Acts and you find this template filled in, city by city. The apostolic gospel is not an overgrowth on Jesus’ teaching. It is his teaching, unsealed.

One covenant, one gospel

Reformed theology confesses one covenant of grace running through the whole of Scripture: the same salvation promised in Eden, pictured in Israel, accomplished at Calvary and proclaimed to the nations. Because there is one God, one Mediator and one saving purpose, the message of Jesus and the message of his apostles cannot be two competing religions. They are two stages of one work.

That is why the older liberalism, for all its learning, misread the evidence so badly. It assumed that doctrine is a corruption of experience, so that Paul’s theology of the cross must be a colder later layer over the warm ethics of Jesus. But Scripture knows nothing of a gospel without a cross. Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51) and said he came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The apostles simply announce what he came to do. The difference between them is not doctrine against experience but promise and fulfilment.

Marcion’s temptation

The wedge is not merely academic. In the second century Marcion tried to sever the God of Jesus from the God of the Old Testament, and even to cut Paul loose from the other apostles, keeping only what fitted his scheme. The church rejected him, and in doing so confessed that the whole Bible tells one story with one Saviour.

Every generation faces some version of Marcion’s temptation: to keep the Jesus we like and quietly discard the rest. Today it looks like the believer who loves the red letters but skims the Epistles as though Paul were an intrusion, or the church that preaches a kind, accepting Jesus but grows embarrassed by the cross and the call to repent. The remedy is not to love Jesus less but to trust him more — enough to receive the apostles he appointed, and to hear in their words the message he sent them to preach.

For reflection

Have you ever felt a gap between the Jesus of the Gospels and the gospel of Paul? Where did that come from? How do Galatians 1:11–12 and Luke 24:46–47 answer it? In what ways might you be tempted to keep only the parts of Christ you prefer?

2.title: “The Kingdom Is at Hand” — Jesus’ Own Proclamation
2.essay:
Mark sums up the whole ministry of Jesus in one sentence of preaching: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15). Every word is loaded.

The hour has come

“The time is fulfilled” uses a word for the appointed, decisive moment — not clock time ticking by, but the hour God had marked on the calendar of redemption. Centuries of Israel’s waiting bend toward this instant. “At hand” means has come near, has drawn up close. The kingdom is not a distant rumour; it is at the door in the person of the one speaking. And notice the word Jesus uses for his own message: the gospel. Before a single apostle preaches, Jesus is already calling his announcement good news.

Then comes the response: repent and believe. It is exactly what the apostles will later demand. Peter says, “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins” (Acts 2:38); Paul testified “of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20:21). The gospel’s summons does not change across the cross; only the fullness of what is believed. From the first sermon to the last, the door into the kingdom is a turned heart that trusts.

The kingdom walking

“Kingdom” on Jesus’ lips is not first a place but a reign: the active, saving rule of God. Where God reigns, demons flee, the sick are healed, sins are forgiven and the poor hear good news. That is why Jesus can say, “the kingdom of God is in the midst of you” (Luke 17:21). The King is standing there. To meet Jesus is to meet the kingdom walking.

In the synagogue at Nazareth he read Isaiah’s promise of good news to the poor, liberty to captives and sight to the blind, and then, with every eye on him, said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21). The prophet’s long-awaited year of the Lord’s favour had walked into the room and sat down. That is the shape of his whole proclamation: in him the promises are being kept now. And it is grace before it is demand — good news to the poor, not a ladder for the strong.

The veil

Yet there is a veil over his preaching before the cross. Again and again he silences demons, and even his disciples, who would announce him too soon (Mark 8:30; 9:9). This restraint, often called the “messianic secret”, is not evasion but timing. The people longed for a conquering king. Jesus would reign, but through a cross, and the meaning of his messiahship could only be safely revealed once that cross had been raised.

The crowds wanted a king who would drive out Rome and spread a banquet of national glory. When Jesus spoke of a kingdom that comes through a cross, “many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him” (John 6:66). The reign he announced was real, but it did not match their appetite for power.

The cross at dawn

So the cross is present in Jesus’ preaching, but in shadow. “The Son of Man must suffer many things” (Mark 8:31). “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). And above all: “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). A ransom is a price paid to set captives free; “for many” echoes the suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, who bears the sins of many. In one sentence, well before Calvary, Jesus interprets his death as a substitutionary, liberating price.

That is not Paul’s later theory imported backward. It is the Lord’s own explanation of why he came. When Paul writes that Christ “gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6), he is echoing his Master. The apostles would preach the cross in broad daylight. Jesus preaches it at dawn — real, certain, but not yet finished.

Herald and content

Two truths must be held together. Jesus is the herald of the kingdom: he proclaims that God’s saving reign has drawn near. And he is its content: the reign draws near because the King has come, and it will be established through his death and resurrection. To set his preaching of the kingdom against the apostles’ preaching of the cross is to miss that the kingdom comes precisely by way of that cross.

This is the “already and not yet” of the whole New Testament. In Jesus the kingdom has truly arrived — sins are forgiven, Satan is bound, the dead are raised — yet its completion waits. The King must first be enthroned by dying before his reign can be preached openly to the nations. Everything Jesus says leans toward that hour.

We are tempted to make the same edit as the crowds. We prize the Jesus who heals and blesses and speaks of a better world, and grow quiet about the Jesus who says he must suffer and calls us to take up a cross. But there is no kingdom without the King, and no King without his cross.

For reflection

What does it mean that the kingdom is first a reign rather than a place? Why did Jesus keep his messiahship veiled before the cross? How does Mark 10:45 show that the theology of the cross began with Jesus himself? Which half of Jesus are you more tempted to keep quiet about?

3.title: The Hinge — Cross, Resurrection, and Pentecost
3.essay:
Why does the form of the message shift at all? Why do the Gospels sound like Galilee and the Epistles like Golgotha? Not because someone changed the message, but because between them stands an event. After the death, resurrection and exaltation of Jesus, no honest witness could preach in the same tense as before.

You cannot announce as finished what has not happened

Before the cross, the decisive act was still future. The disciples could not yet preach “Christ died for our sins and rose again”, because he had not yet died and risen. The shift from Gospels to Epistles is a shift of place on the timeline of redemption, not a change of gospel. Revelation unfolds through the events it describes, so the message about those events deepens as they happen. Before the cross the accent falls on the King who has come and the reign that is dawning; after the resurrection it falls on the finished work and the enthroned Lord. Same Christ, same grace, same kingdom, now proclaimed from the far side of the empty tomb.

The resurrection

The resurrection is the great hinge. It does not merely reverse the crucifixion; it vindicates and enthrones the Crucified. Paul opens Romans by defining “the gospel of God” as news about a person: the Son, descended from David, “declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4). Set that beside Mark’s first line — “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mark 1:1) — and the unity is plain. Mark calls the story of Jesus the gospel; Paul calls the risen Jesus the gospel.

At Pentecost Peter reached the summit of the first Christian sermon: “Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36). Peter does not say God made Jesus divine, as though he became something he was not. He says God has publicly installed and vindicated the crucified Jesus as reigning Lord and Messiah. Heaven has given its verdict on the cross, and the verdict is a throne. Jesus had announced that God’s reign was at hand; now Peter announces that the King has taken his seat. So the message has a new key: no longer “the kingdom is coming”, but “the King has been enthroned; come to him.”

Minds opened

The apostles did not understand the cross even as it approached; they scattered. On the road to Emmaus two disciples walked in despair: “But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21) — past tense, hope buried. Then the risen Christ opened the Scriptures to them, and their hearts burned within them.

That evening, two things happened that made the apostolic gospel possible. “Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45): the same slow-hearted disciples were given the understanding to read the whole Old Testament as pointing to a suffering and rising Messiah. And he commissioned the message: repentance and forgiveness, in his name, to all nations (Luke 24:47). The apostles did not compose their gospel; they received it, already formed, from the mouth of the risen Lord. Luke 24 is the true seam of the Bible. Pentecost would supply the power; Luke 24 supplied the content.

The Spirit of truth

Jesus had promised, “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth … He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:13–14). The poured-out Spirit filled the apostles with power and understanding. Their gospel is not a human reconstruction of half-remembered sayings. It is the same Lord interpreting his own finished work through the Spirit he sent.

So the apostles are not free authors improving on Jesus. They are his authorised witnesses, taught by the risen Christ and carried by his Spirit. “The one who hears you hears me” (Luke 10:16). To receive the apostolic gospel is not to leave Jesus behind for his followers. It is to keep listening to Jesus, speaking now through the men he commissioned and the Spirit he poured out.

Living on the far side

We live entirely on the far side of the hinge. We have never known the message in its pre-Easter form; we receive it as the apostles preached it, from an empty tomb. That is a mercy. We are not left to piece together a religion from scattered sayings. We are handed the finished gospel by eyewitnesses whom the risen Lord himself taught. When we read Paul, we are not straying from Jesus. We are hearing Jesus’ own commission carried out.

For reflection

Why could the disciples not preach the cross and resurrection before they happened? What does Acts 2:36 tell us about what the resurrection changed? Read Luke 24:13–49: what does the risen Jesus give his disciples? How should it shape your reading of the Epistles that the apostles were taught by the risen Christ?

4.title: The Apostolic Kerygma — “Christ Died for Our Sins”
4.essay:
When we ask what the apostles actually preached, we are not left to guess. Paul preserves the earliest Christian creed, older than any of his letters, handed to him and now handed to us.

Of first importance

“For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve” (1 Corinthians 15:3–5). Death, burial, resurrection, appearances: this is the irreducible core, and Paul says it is what he received, not what he devised. It was likely fixed within a few years of the resurrection. That alone answers the charge that the cross-centred gospel was a late invention. Long before there was a New Testament, the church was confessing that Christ died for our sins and rose on the third day.

Weigh the phrase “for our sins”. The death is not a tragedy to be explained away but a substitution to be received. And “in accordance with the Scriptures” ties it to Isaiah’s Servant and the whole Old Testament hope — the very Scriptures Jesus opened in Luke 24.

The pattern in Acts

The sermons in Acts show the same pattern, city by city. Whether it is Peter at Pentecost or Paul in the synagogue at Antioch, the shape recurs: the age of promise has been fulfilled; Jesus lived, taught and did mighty works; he was crucified according to God’s plan; God raised and exalted him; therefore repent, believe and receive forgiveness. Scholars call this the apostolic kerygma, “the thing preached”. It is remarkably stable, which is why it reads like one gospel in many voices. It is the commission of Luke 24 filled out in history.

Peter holds two truths in one sentence: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. God raised him up” (Acts 2:23–24). The cross was the darkest crime in history and the deliberate plan of God. The “must” of the Gospels — “the Son of Man must suffer” (Mark 8:31) — has become the “definite plan” of Acts. The apostles are announcing that what Jesus said had to happen has happened.

What shall we do?

At Pentecost the hearers “were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, ‘Brothers, what shall we do?’” (Acts 2:37). Peter’s answer — repent, be baptised, receive forgiveness — is the summons Jesus began with in Galilee. Three thousand were added that day. The apostolic gospel was not a colder religion than Jesus’; it was fire. A gospel that stops at Jesus the teacher, without his death for our sins and his resurrection, has no answer to that cry. It can inspire, but it cannot forgive.

Justification unfolds the cross

Out of this core the great doctrines of the Epistles unfold. Justification by faith is not an alien addition; it is the courtroom meaning of “Christ died for our sins”. If he bore our sins and rose, the verdict over the believing sinner is acquittal: “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24). Reconciliation, redemption and adoption are not additions either, but the same cross applied to the guilty conscience.

So Paul and Jesus preach one grace. Jesus welcomed sinners and pronounced their sins forgiven by his own authority (Mark 2:5; Luke 7:48). Paul explains that this forgiveness rests on the cross and is received by faith alone. The tax collector “went down to his house justified” in Luke’s Gospel (Luke 18:14) before Paul ever wrote Romans. The grace is identical; the apostles show us its ground and its glory.

They never stopped preaching the kingdom

Here is the detail that quietly dismantles the slogan that “Jesus preached the kingdom, the church preached Christ”: the apostles never stopped preaching the kingdom. Philip “preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts 8:12). Paul reasoned about it in Ephesus for three months (Acts 19:8). And Luke ends his two volumes with Paul in Rome, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance” (Acts 28:31).

Those are not two subjects but one. The kingdom is the reign of God now inaugurated in the enthroned Jesus. To preach Christ as Lord is to preach the kingdom come. The kingdom did not disappear from apostolic preaching. It arrived, in the King they proclaimed.

For reflection

Why does it matter that 1 Corinthians 15:3–5 is so early? Read Peter’s sermon in Acts 2: which parts of the kerygma can you find? How is justification by faith the “courtroom meaning” of the cross? Why is a gospel without the cross unable to answer “What shall we do?”

5.title: One Gospel, Two Moments — The Deep Unity
5.essay:
Now we can say plainly what unites Jesus and the apostles. It is not that their messages merely overlap. They preach one gospel at two moments on the single timeline of redemption — the difference between “the kingdom of God is at hand” and “It is finished”.

Threads across the seam

Jesus announces the reign of God arriving in himself and moving toward its climax at the cross. The apostles announce that the climax has come, the King is enthroned and salvation is accomplished and offered to the world. Promise and fulfilment — but one promise, one fulfilment, one Christ. And several threads run unbroken across the seam.

The response is the same: Jesus calls for repentance and faith (Mark 1:15), and so do the apostles (Acts 20:21). The grace is the same: Jesus gives the kingdom to the poor in spirit and the desperate tax collector, not the self-assured; Paul declares salvation “by grace … through faith … not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9). Neither leaves room for a boast. The Scriptures are the same: Jesus reads Isaiah and says, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled” (Luke 4:21); Paul preaches Christ “in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3). Both open the same Old Testament and find the same Messiah. And above all, the Christ is the same.

Forgiveness in person

Long before Paul writes about justification, Jesus does what justification describes. To a paralysed man let down through a roof he says, “Son, your sins are forgiven” (Mark 2:5). The scribes are scandalised: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:7). They are right about the premise and wrong about the man. The one standing before them is God with us, and he dispenses pardon as freely as he heals a body. Paul gives us the ground of that pardon, the cross, and the means, faith. Jesus gives us the reality in person. Same forgiveness, one Saviour.

The tax collector went home justified

The word Paul made famous first appears on Jesus’ lips. A tax collector, unable even to lift his eyes, beats his breast and prays, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” Jesus says, “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other” (Luke 18:13–14). Not the religious man with his record of works, but the empty-handed sinner who casts himself on mercy, is declared right with God. Justification by faith is not Paul’s invention; it is Jesus’ parable.

Notice the plea itself. “Be merciful to me” carries the sense “let atonement be made for me”, the language of the mercy seat where blood was sprinkled for sin. Without knowing all it would mean, the tax collector asks for exactly what the cross would provide, and Jesus grants it. When we read his prayer and then read Romans, the seam should vanish. The sinner who beats his breast and the sinner Paul calls “justified by faith” are the same person receiving the same mercy.

Grace and kingdom in one breath

In his farewell to the Ephesian elders, Paul describes his life’s work as testifying “to the gospel of the grace of God” and, in the next sentence, as “proclaiming the kingdom” (Acts 20:24–25). For Paul these are one ministry. The reign of God and the grace of God meet in the crucified and risen King. If the apostle to the Gentiles can describe his work both ways in one breath, then Jesus’ kingdom-preaching and Paul’s grace-preaching were never rivals.

When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus really was the Coming One, Jesus’ answer was Isaiah come to life: the blind see, the lame walk, “the poor have good news preached to them” (Luke 7:22). That was the kingdom, and it was pure grace to the helpless — the same grace the apostles preach when they say Christ died for the ungodly.

The King reigns from the tree

The unity of the two moments rests on the unity of the Christ. The kingdom of God and the cross of Christ are not competing centres but one reality seen from two angles: the King reigns from the tree. Calvary is not an interruption of the kingdom but its throne room. Lifted up on the cross, he is enthroned; raised, he is vindicated; ascended, he takes his seat at the right hand. The reign he announced in Galilee is established by the death and resurrection the apostles proclaim.

So Jesus is the herald who is also the message. In the Gospels he proclaims the gospel; in the Epistles he is the gospel proclaimed. He does not stand outside his message pointing to it; he is its heart. To divide his kingdom-preaching from the apostles’ Christ-preaching is finally to divide Jesus from himself. This is deeply freeing. We do not have to choose between the Jesus of the Gospels and the gospel of the apostles. To fall at his feet crying, “Be merciful to me,” is the gospel of grace — preached by the King and explained by his witnesses.

For reflection

Which of the threads across the seam — response, grace, Scriptures, Christ — strikes you most? How does Mark 2:1–12 show Jesus doing what justification describes? Read Luke 18:9–14 and Romans 4:1–8 side by side. What do you notice? What does it mean that “the King reigns from the tree”?

6.title: Guarding the One Gospel Today
6.essay:
If Jesus and the apostles preach one gospel at two moments, then two errors wait on either side of the road, and both are alive in the church today. Understanding the unity is not just an academic settlement. It is a guardrail for the soul and the pulpit.

Jesus without the cross

The first error keeps Jesus and loses the cross. It prizes the red letters — the teacher of love and justice and the beautiful ideals of the kingdom — but grows embarrassed by substitutionary death, by wrath and atonement, by the call to repent. It is Harnack’s ghost in modern dress: a Jesus of ethics without the Saviour who bled. But a kingdom with no cross has no doorway. A Christ who only instructs cannot forgive. Strip the atonement out of Jesus and you are left with a moral example who condemns you by his very perfection and cannot save you at all.

The cross without the kingdom

The second error keeps the cross and loses the kingdom. It reduces the gospel to a private transaction — my sins forgiven, my ticket to heaven — and never bows before the crucified King as Lord of every part of life. But the apostles never preached a cross without a crown. The same Paul who preached Christ crucified preached the kingdom of God to the end (Acts 28:31).

Paul joins them in one sentence

“He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” (Colossians 1:13–14). To be saved is to be transferred into the kingdom — the language of Jesus’ Galilean preaching — and in the same clause to have redemption and forgiveness — the language of the cross. They are one salvation described from two angles. You do not enter the kingdom apart from the forgiveness the cross secures, and you are not forgiven except into the reign of the beloved Son. That answers both errors at once. Against the cross-less kingdom: entry comes only through redemption. Against the kingdom-less cross: forgiveness lands us under a King, owing him everything.

The Great Commission

The Great Commission joins the two moments in one scene. The crucified and risen Jesus says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18) — the enthroned King, the kingdom come in power. From that throne he sends his apostles to make disciples of all nations, to baptise and to teach obedience to everything he commanded, and he promises, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The gospel the apostles preach is Jesus’ gospel, carried under his authority and empowered by his presence. There is no seam between the Christ who commands and the church that obeys.

The Lamb on the throne

The Bible’s final vision gathers every thread into one song. At the centre of heaven’s worship stands a Lamb, looking as though it had been slain: cross and throne in one image. The elders sing, “Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth” (Revelation 5:9–10). He is worshipped because by his blood he ransomed a people — Mark 10:45 come to full glory — and because that ransomed people will reign with him. This is where Jesus’ preaching and the apostles’ preaching were always heading.

The good deposit

Scripture calls this gospel a sacred trust: “By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you” (2 Timothy 1:14). When Paul handed the gospel on to Timothy, he did not hand him a private religion or a bare kingdom ethic. He charged him “in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom” (2 Timothy 4:1). Cross and kingdom in one charge, passed from the apostle to the next generation, exactly as they had come from Christ to the apostle.

Every heresy that has troubled the church has in some way torn apart what Jesus and his apostles held together: law from grace, grace from lordship, the Jesus of history from the Christ of faith. Faithfulness means keeping the seam sealed.

On our knees

The deposit is now in our hands, and we are still tempted to keep the half of Christ we prefer: a gentle teacher without a cross, or a personal Saviour without a throne. The gospel of Jesus and his apostles will not be halved. It offers a crucified King who forgives our sins, reigns over our lives and will fill the earth with his glory.

So this study ends not at the desk but on our knees. If Jesus is the herald who is also the message, the right response to both his preaching and his apostles’ is the one the tax collector gave, the one Pentecost drew out, the one the Great Commission commands: repent, believe, and follow the crucified and risen King. There is one gospel, one Christ, one grace, and he bids us come.

For reflection

Which of the two errors — Jesus without the cross, or the cross without the kingdom — are you or your church more prone to? How does Colossians 1:13–14 correct both? Read Revelation 5 aloud. How does it gather together everything in this study? What would it mean for you to “guard the good deposit” this week?
